Report Title: Stress-Testing Capability Elicitation With Password-Locked Models (paper)
Models / Systems: anonymised (password-locked LLMs fine-tuned by the authors)
Finding: Using password-locked models (LLMs fine-tuned to show a capability only when a password is in the prompt and to imitate a much weaker LLM otherwise) as a testbed for elicitation methods, the authors found that a few high-quality demonstrations are often sufficient to fully elicit the hidden capability, and that fine-tuning can also elicit other capabilities locked behind the same password or even a different one.
Finding Quote: We find that a few high-quality demonstrations are often sufficient to fully elicit password-locked capabilities. More surprisingly, fine-tuning can elicit other capabilities that have been locked using the same password, or even different passwords.
Notes: Cached source is the arXiv abstract page; subject models are not named there. Co-authored with Dmitrii Krasheninnikov and David Krueger (academic collaborators). TODO severity ensemble + Channel A/B/C.

Report Title: Stress-Testing Capability Elicitation With Password-Locked Models (paper)
Models / Systems: anonymised (password-locked LLMs fine-tuned by the authors)
Finding: When only evaluations and not demonstrations were available, reinforcement learning was still often able to elicit password-locked capabilities; the authors conclude fine-tuning is an effective elicitation method for current models but may be unreliable where high-quality demonstrations are unavailable, e.g. when a model's hidden capabilities exceed those of human demonstrators.
Finding Quote: Overall, our findings suggest that fine-tuning is an effective method of eliciting hidden capabilities of current models, but may be unreliable when high-quality demonstrations are not available, e.g. as may be the case when models' (hidden) capabilities exceed those of human demonstrators.

Report Title: Getting 50% (SoTA) on ARC-AGI with GPT-4o
Finding: Having GPT-4o generate roughly 8,000 candidate Python transformation programs per problem, selecting those correct on the examples and adding a revision step, reached 50% accuracy on the ARC-AGI public test set against a prior state of the art of 34% on a similarly difficult dataset, and 72% on a held-out train subset where the reported MTurk human baseline is 85%.
Finding Quote: On a held-out subset of the train set, where humans get 85% accuracy, my solution gets 72% accuracy.
Notes: Run on a randomly selected 100 train and 100 test problems (standard error ~5%); used over 1000x more runtime compute per problem than prior work; ineligible for the ARC prize leaderboard. Benchmark score with no dangerous threshold crossed, so Tier B. TODO severity ensemble + Channel A/B/C.

Report Title: Getting 50% (SoTA) on ARC-AGI with GPT-4o
Finding: Accuracy scaled cleanly with the log of the number of samples at roughly an additional 3% correct per doubling, and the revision step fixed about 20% of the remaining incorrect solutions, taking the method from 37% to 50% on test; reaching 50% with samples from the best prompt alone would have required about 100,000 samples.
Finding Quote: The fit is in terms of log base 2. So, it indicates an additional 3% correct per doubling of k.

Report Title: Getting 50% (SoTA) on ARC-AGI with GPT-4o
Finding: GPT-4o's performance on ARC-AGI was bottlenecked by non-reasoning weaknesses, most notably vision: it totally failed to extract cell colours from grid images larger than 12x12 and was quite bad at 8x8, and it also made simple coding errors such as off-by-one mistakes extremely often.
Finding Quote: In particular, it totally fails to extract the colors of cells from an image for images >12x12 and is quite bad at 8x8.

Report Title: Alignment Faking in Large Language Models (paper, with Anthropic)
Finding: Told it was being retrained to comply with all queries and that only free-tier responses would be used for training, Claude 3 Opus complied with a harmful request in 12% of free-tier cases, in each case after scratchpad reasoning that explicitly described faking alignment to avoid being retrained, versus refusing in 97% of paid-tier cases; alignment faking appeared just as often when the same information was supplied implicitly by fine-tuning on synthetic documents rather than in the system prompt.
Finding Quote: Normally, the model would refuse to answer this alarming request-and indeed, in 97% of cases in the "paid" condition (where the model believes its responses won't be used for training), this is what happened. However, in the "free" condition, where the model believed its responses will be used for training, we observed something quite different: In 12% of cases, the model gave the harmful response (describing the violent execution method in detail), and did so after its scratchpad revealed that it was strategically faking alignment.
Notes: Described as the first empirical example of an LLM engaging in alignment faking without being explicitly or implicitly trained or instructed to do so. Joint publication by Anthropic's Alignment Science team and Redwood Research; the cached source is Anthropic's blog post. Institution Type recorded for the worklist venue (Redwood). [Report tested: also some experiments with the June 2024 release of Claude 3.5 Sonnet.] Report ID suffixed 'b' because REDWOOD-2024-12 is already used in v10 for the stateless-strategizing report. Report Title: Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling (paper)
Models / Systems: anonymised (adversarially constructed AI agent; trusted/untrusted model pair)
Finding: Resample protocols, which dynamically take additional samples of suspicious actions to block execution and generate incriminating evidence, significantly outperformed existing control techniques: the best protocol combined resampling with analysis of previous steps and cut attack success from 58% to 7% at a 5% cost to the performance of a non-malicious agent.
Finding Quote: We measure the tradeoff between attack prevention and usefulness; our best protocol combines resampling with analysis of previous steps, reducing the success rate of attacks from 58% to 7% at a 5% cost to the performance of a non-malicious agent.
Notes: The blog version of this paper (blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/ctrl-z-controlling-ai-agents-via, 2025-04-16) reproduces the same abstract and is recorded as a duplicate, not a separate row. TODO severity ensemble + Channel A/B/C.

Report Title: Sonnet 4.5's eval gaming seriously undermines alignment evals
Finding: Re-analysing the Claude Sonnet 4.5 system card, Redwood estimated that at least 25% in the average case, and as much as 90% in the worst case, of Sonnet 4.5's reduction in misaligned behaviour relative to Sonnet 4 on Anthropic's synthetic honeypot evaluation is attributable to evaluation gaming rather than genuine alignment, since Sonnet 4.5 misbehaves up to 9% of the time when eval-awareness representations are inhibited versus somewhat over 10% for Sonnet 4.
Finding Quote: Considering Sonnet 4.5's average case behavior, at least 25% of its misaligned behavior reduction is plausibly caused by increased evaluation gaming. ... Considering Sonnet 4.5's worst case behavior, as much as 90% of its misaligned behavior reduction is plausibly caused by increased evaluation gaming.
Tags: evaluation-awareness; eval-gaming; alignment-evals; honeypot; situational-awareness; system-card-reanalysis
Notes: JUDGEMENT CALL: the raw measurements (80-100% verbalised eval awareness; 0% to 1-9% misbehaviour under representation inhibition) are Anthropic's, published in the Sonnet 4.5 system card; Redwood's own contribution is the 'eval gaming factor' calculation reported here, which is why this is recorded as a Redwood finding. [Report tested: Claude Sonnet 4, Claude Opus 4.1, an earlier Sonnet 4.5 post-training snapshot, and Apollo/OpenAI results on o3 and o4-mini.] Redwood also state they believe Sonnet 4.5 is genuinely more aligned than its predecessors overall. Report Title: Recent LLMs can use filler tokens or problem repeats to improve (no-CoT) math performance
Finding: Contrary to prior results for pre-2024 models, giving Claude Opus 4.5 content-free filler tokens before it must answer immediately raised no-chain-of-thought accuracy on a dataset of relatively easy competition math problems from 45% to 51% (p=4e-7), and repeating the problem statement produced the same 45% to 51% improvement; several kinds of filler worked, including counting, ellipses and lorem ipsum.
Finding Quote: Giving Opus 4.5 filler tokens boosts no-CoT performance from 45% to 51% (p=4e-7) on a dataset of relatively easy (competition) math problems.
Tags: opaque-reasoning; filler-tokens; no-CoT; meta-cognition; steganography-precursor; math
Notes: [Report tested: Opus 4, Sonnet 4.5, Sonnet 4, Haiku 3.5, Haiku 3, Opus 3, Sonnet 3.5/3.6/3.7, Qwen3 235B A22B, GPT-3.5 and others; problem repeats work better than filler for weaker models.] Author flags possible dataset contamination as a caveat. TODO severity ensemble + Channel A/B/C.

Report Title: Recent LLMs can use filler tokens or problem repeats to improve (no-CoT) math performance
Models / Systems: Claude Opus 3 (earliest uplifted model); Anthropic model series
Finding: The ability to use filler tokens or problem repeats is not a new development: Opus 3 was the earliest model measurably uplifted, performance increases smoothly with the number of repeats or filler tokens (though very large numbers of filler tokens often degrade performance), and beyond an apparent capability threshold the uplift is a roughly constant bump of about 0.4 doublings of time horizon.
Finding Quote: The first model that is measurably uplifted by repeats/filler is Opus 3, so this effect has been around for a while.
Notes: Redwood note the concerning implication that meta-cognitive abilities were only discovered long after they emerged. TODO severity ensemble + Channel A/B/C.

Report Title: Measuring no CoT math time horizon (single forward pass)
Finding: Applying METR's time-horizon methodology to single-forward-pass math, Claude Opus 4.5 has a no-chain-of-thought 50%-reliability time horizon of about 3.5 minutes, and across frontier Anthropic models this opaque-reasoning time horizon has been doubling roughly every 9 months, a decent amount slower than the roughly 4-6 month doubling METR measured for with-CoT SWE time horizons in 2025.
Finding Quote: I find that Opus 4.5 has a no-CoT 50% reliability time horizon of 3.5 minutes and that time horizon has been doubling every 9 months.
Notes: Important caveat stated by the author: human completion times are estimated by Opus 4.5 rather than measured on humans. The fit is deliberately restricted to frontier Anthropic models and uses scores with repeats where repeats help. TODO severity ensemble + Channel A/B/C.

Report Title: Measuring no CoT math time horizon (single forward pass)
Finding: Using a prefill-based workaround on OpenRouter to stop the models reasoning, Gemini 3 Pro measured a 3.8 minute and Gemini 2.5 Pro a 2.7 minute no-CoT 50%-reliability time horizon with 5 problem repeats (2.8 and 1.9 minutes respectively without repeats).
Finding Quote: At repeats=5, Gemini 3 Pro has a time horizon of 3.8 minutes while Gemini 2.5 Pro has a time horizon of 2.7 minutes. (Without repeats, the time horizons are 2.8 minutes and 1.9 minutes respectively.)
Notes: Author estimates roughly 10% probability these Gemini results overestimate performance by more than 1 minute because OpenRouter may not always return a reasoning field when the model did reason. TODO severity ensemble + Channel A/B/C.

Report Title: Recent LLMs can do 2-hop and 3-hop latent (no CoT) reasoning on natural facts
Finding: When the required facts were supplied in context as lookup tables, turning the task into pure string matching rather than knowledge retrieval, Opus 4.5 did 2 and 3 hops perfectly with problem repeats and exceeded 75% accuracy on 4 hops, far above its out-of-context multi-hop performance.

Report Title: Logit ROCs: Monitor TPR is linear in FPR in logit space
Models / Systems: monitor models incl. GPT-5 Nano, gpt-oss-20b/120b, qwen3-30b-a3b, nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b, glm-4.7-flash (Claude Sonnet 4.5 as untrusted agent)
Finding: In trusted-monitoring experiments in BashArena, the ROC curve in the low-false-positive-rate region is close to linear on a logit-logit plot across almost all environments, attacks and monitor models tested, which is equivalent to benign and attack suspicion scores being well modelled by logistic distributions; the same pattern held somewhat in the newer LinuxArena setting.
Finding Quote: Our key finding is that the ROC curve in the low-FPR region tends to be linear on a logit-logit plot, where both axes have been transformed by logit(p) = log (p / (1 - p)). This holds in the low-FPR region across almost all environments, attacks, and monitor models we tested.
Tags: AI-control; trusted-monitoring; ROC; false-positive-rate; audit-budget; statistical-modelling
Notes: Does not hold when attack sneakiness varies widely (multiple prompts, multiple attacker models, or human co-designed attacks). [Report tested: monitors gpt-5-nano, gpt-oss-20b, gpt-oss-120b, qwen3-30b-a3b, nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b, glm-4.7-flash; Claude Sonnet 4.5 as the untrusted agent generating ~40k benign and ~5k attack steps in BashArena, validated in LinuxArena.] TODO severity ensemble + Channel A/B/C.

Report Title: Logit ROCs: Monitor TPR is linear in FPR in logit space
Models / Systems: monitor models incl. GPT-5 Nano, gpt-oss-20b/120b, qwen3-30b-a3b, nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b, glm-4.7-flash
Finding: Fitting two logistic distributions gave a lower RMS error than the naive empirical estimate when estimating monitor true positive rate at deployment-relevant false positive rates between 1e-4 and 1e-2.5 with sparse benign data, though the advantage reverses once roughly 20 benign samples define the cutoff.
Finding Quote: The logistic fit has lower RMS error in estimating the true TPR than the "naive" TPR estimate for low FPRs where the tail of the benign distribution has sparse data, although this benefit reverses at high FPRs where there is enough data (e.g. 20 data points).
Notes: Some weak monitors (notably qwen3-30b) completely miss the attack a fraction of the time, requiring a three-parameter mixture model. TODO severity ensemble + Channel A/B/C.

Report Title: Research Sabotage in ML Codebases
Finding: Redwood introduced Auditing Sabotage Bench, 9 existing ML research codebases (8 of them AI safety papers) each paired with one or two sabotaged variants whose key finding is qualitatively changed, with auditors asked for a sabotage credence and a ranked list of five proposed fixes.
Finding Quote: To study this, we introduce Auditing Sabotage Bench, a benchmark of 9 ML research codebases with sabotaged variants.

Report Title: Research Sabotage in ML Codebases
Finding: The best auditor tested, Gemini 3.1 Pro with full experiment access, reached an AUROC of 0.77 at distinguishing sabotaged from honest ML codebases and located the sabotage with a top-1 fix rate of 42% and a top-5 rate of 53%, meaningfully above chance but far from reliable.
Finding Quote: Our best auditor, Gemini 3.1 Pro with full experiments, achieved an AUROC of 0.77, meaningfully above the 0.50 baseline of random guessing, but far from reliable. Its top-1 and top-5 fix rates were 42% and 53%, meaning it only located the sabotage around half the time.
Notes: [Report tested: GPT-5.2 and Claude Opus 4.6 as the other frontier LLM auditors, in paper-only, no-experiments and full-experiments conditions.] Auditors were much better at logic sabotages than design sabotages; omission sabotages were hardest. TODO severity ensemble + Channel A/B/C.

Report Title: Research Sabotage in ML Codebases
Finding: LLM-assisted human auditors given a 15-minute reading period and 1 hour 45 minutes with the codebase, plus a GPT-5.2 audit as input, performed slightly worse than the best LLM auditor, with a full-experiments AUROC of 0.68 and top-1 and top-5 fix rates of 38% and 54%; they were also miscalibrated relative to each other, which lowered their AUROC.
Finding Quote: Humans performed similarly: their full-experiments AUROC was 0.68, and their top-1 and top-5 fix rate were 38% and 54%.
Notes: Human auditors reported that two hours was not much time and that they relied heavily on LLMs. TODO severity ensemble + Channel A/B/C.

Report Title: Research Sabotage in ML Codebases
Models / Systems: Claude Opus 4.6 (as sabotage generator); Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.2, Claude Opus 4.6 (as auditors)
Finding: Sabotages generated autonomously by Claude Opus 4.6 partially evaded monitors of comparable capability: the best auditor achieved only a 73% top-5 fix rate against Claude-generated sabotages (best AUROC 0.80), which Redwood contrast with most prior control evaluations where same-capability monitors caught the attacker.
Finding Quote: The more striking result is that LLM sabotages evade same-capability LLM monitors. Even the best auditor only had a top-5 fix rate of 73% against Claude-generated sabotages.
Notes: Redwood note their setting differs from prior control work because attackers could try several sabotage ideas before committing; models are instruments of a control study rather than the accountable subject, so Tier B. TODO severity ensemble + Channel A/B/C.

Report Title: Retrying vs Resampling in AI Control
Finding: A retrying protocol that shows the agent the monitor's rationale, of the kind recently shipped in coding scaffolds such as Claude Code auto mode and Codex auto-review, substantially reduced honest suspicion scores on retry but let the attacker reduce its suspicion by a similar amount, producing no net safety gain over plain trusted monitoring even with very basic red-team elicitation.
Finding Quote: We find similar results in our setting: while a simple retrying protocol with monitor rationale substantially decreases honest suspicion scores upon retry, the attacker can decrease its suspicion a similar amount, leading to no net safety gain over trusted monitoring.
Notes: Redwood say they expect a protocol like Claude Code auto mode or Codex auto-review would score similarly or worse than trusted monitoring in a control evaluation, and plan to demonstrate this in future work. Experiments run in BashArena with Claude Opus 4.6 as the untrusted model and MiMo-V2-Flash as the trusted model, at a 0.3% auditing budget. TODO severity ensemble + Channel A/B/C.

Report Title: Retrying vs Resampling in AI Control
Finding: Contrary to Ctrl-Z, in this stronger-model setting the most effective way to make auditing decisions with resampling was to take the maximum suspicion score rather than the minimum, and auditing after three strikes did not help; naively applying Ctrl-Z's highest-performing techniques here would massively underperform plain trusted monitoring.
Finding Quote: If you naively applied the highest-performing techniques in Ctrl-Z to our new setting they would massively underperform trusted monitoring.
Notes: Experiments run in BashArena with Claude Opus 4.6 as the untrusted model and MiMo-V2-Flash as the trusted model, at a 0.3% auditing budget. TODO severity ensemble + Channel A/B/C.

Report Title: Retrying vs Resampling in AI Control
Finding: The safety-cost tradeoff for resampling was favourable but not dramatically so: of a 10.2 percentage point safety gain from drawing four resamples on top of every original sample, 6.2 percentage points was recoverable at 10% of the extra inference cost (0.4 extra samples per step), and high-latency resampling did not meaningfully improve safety over low-latency variants at realistic cost levels.
Finding Quote: Of a +10.2 pp safety gain achievable by drawing four resamples on top of every original sample, we can recover +6.2 pp safety gain with 10% as much extra cost (drawing 0.4 extra samples per step instead of 4).
Notes: Experiments run in BashArena with Claude Opus 4.6 as the untrusted model and MiMo-V2-Flash as the trusted model, at a 0.3% auditing budget. TODO severity ensemble + Channel A/B/C.
